system.name: recipe-share
system.description: Recipe-sharing web app: users publish recipes, browse, comment, and upload photos. 100 registered users, 2 developers, GBP 50/month infrastructure budget.

functional: Users upload photos attached to recipes

assumptions.text: 30% of the 100 registered users are active on a given day (30 DAU), with 2 sessions/day and 40 requests/session.
assumptions.impact: Even at the extreme (100% DAU, 20x peak factor) peak load is 1.9 requests/second; the architecture decision does not change anywhere in the plausible range.

assumptions.text: Peak factor 10: single-timezone consumer app with evening concentration.
assumptions.impact: A lower factor only strengthens the conclusion; a higher one is covered by the sensitivity bound above.

assumptions.text: Content volume: ~3 recipes, ~10 comments, ~6 photos uploaded per day; photos average 3 MB as uploaded, ~4 MB stored including resized derivatives.
assumptions.impact: 5x more photo volume raises object storage to ~45 GB/year, roughly GBP 1-3/month extra. No architectural change.

assumptions.text: Audience is single-region (UK/EU implied by GBP budget); no geographic latency requirement.
assumptions.impact: If a large distant audience appears, image delivery latency becomes the first complaint; the CDN rejection has a trigger for this.

assumptions.text: Team of 2 developers, no dedicated ops; both will operate what they build.
assumptions.impact: Sets the complexity budget at 4 points.

assumptions.text: No availability target stated; minutes of downtime during deploys or platform incidents are acceptable.
assumptions.impact: If wrong and a target near 99.9%+ is actually required, a second instance and a load balancer become justified; see the load-balancer rejection.

assumptions.text: Capacity figures computed by hand from the documented formulas in calculators/README.md; the calculator could not be executed in this environment.
assumptions.impact: Arithmetic is shown with substituted values in the design document so every line can be checked by hand.

components.name: Monolithic web application on a managed platform
components.justification: Peak load is 0.28 requests/second (1.9 at the most extreme plausible inputs) against single-instance comfort of ~10+; one small managed instance has ~2-3 orders of magnitude of headroom. Image resizing runs in-process at upload (~6 photos/day).

components.name: Managed PostgreSQL
components.justification: ~20 writes/day and ~0.02 GB/year of relational data - any relational database handles this with no tuning. Postgres full-text search covers recipe search at this corpus size, and a jobs table covers any future async work at zero additional components. Provider handles backups and point-in-time recovery.

components.name: Managed object storage for photos
components.justification: ~8.8 GB/year of photos at ~11 GB/month egress. Keeping binaries out of the database keeps backups small and restores fast; photos are served directly from storage at these volumes.

rejected_components.reason: Total peak traffic is 0.28 requests/second; no single key comes near the ~10 requests/second threshold at which relieved load becomes measurable, and the origin database is idle. A cache here adds a component and a staleness bug class for no measurable benefit.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Any single query exceeds 10 requests/second sustained over a week, or database CPU exceeds 50% sustained - then compute what a cache would actually relieve before adding it.

rejected_components.reason: Egress is ~11 GB/month against the few-hundred-GB threshold below which edge offload does not repay the component. Most managed platforms include this volume in the base price.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Egress exceeds 200 GB/month for 2 consecutive months, or users in a distant geography report image load latency.

rejected_components.reason: The corpus grows at ~1,000 recipes/year; Postgres full-text search with a GIN index handles this at sub-10ms with zero additional components. A dedicated search engine is 3 points (self-hosted) or 1 point plus a datastore technology (managed) for no measured gap.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Recipe count exceeds 100,000, or search p95 exceeds 500 ms with the query already indexed.

rejected_components.reason: Async workload is ~6 image-resize jobs/day; resizing runs synchronously at upload in ~1-2 seconds. Even the zero-cost fallback (a jobs table in Postgres) is comfortable to roughly 500 jobs/second - a dedicated broker is unjustified by around 7 orders of magnitude.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Job volume exceeds 500 jobs/second sustained at peak over a week - and reach for the database-backed jobs table first when async is needed at all.

rejected_components.reason: Streaming earns its 3-4 points above ~500 events/second sustained or with 3+ independent consumer groups requiring replay. This system has one consumer (itself) and ~20 writes/day.
rejected_components.revisit_when: 3 or more independent consumers need to replay the same activity stream as a confirmed requirement, or sustained event throughput exceeds 500/second.

rejected_components.reason: A separately deployed worker service adds a deploy pipeline and a version boundary (+2 points total) to process ~6 short jobs/day that fit in the request path.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Any job exceeds 5 seconds at p95, or job volume exceeds 1/minute sustained - then move to an in-app background thread or jobs table before a separate service.

rejected_components.reason: One instance serves peak load with ~2-3 orders of magnitude of headroom; there is no second instance to balance across. No availability target was stated that would justify redundancy.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Peak RPS exceeds ~50, or an availability target of 99.9% or above is stated - either justifies a second instance and therefore a balancer.

rejected_components.reason: Peak reads are 0.28/second against the ~1,000/second threshold where offloading reads becomes worth the replication-lag correctness questions.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Reads exceed 1,000/second with a hot working set, measured at the database.

rejected_components.reason: One deployed service and two developers with no dedicated ops. An orchestration platform is 4 points - the team's entire budget - to schedule one container.
rejected_components.revisit_when: 3 or more independently deployed services exist and a dedicated ops engineer is hired.

options.description: Simplest viable option: one monolithic web app on a managed platform (Fly.io/Render/Railway class), managed PostgreSQL, managed object storage for photos. Server-rendered pages; image resize in-process at upload; Postgres full-text search; provider-managed backups with PITR.
trade_offs: Single instance: deploys and platform incidents mean minutes of downtime (~99.5% in practice, no stated target to breach)
Some platform lock-in in deploy config, though the app itself is a portable container
Postgres full-text search is weaker than a dedicated engine for typo-tolerance and relevance tuning
Synchronous image processing ties upload latency to photo size (~1-2 s per photo)

options.description: One VPS running the app, SQLite (or self-installed Postgres), and photos on local disk behind Caddy. Cheapest possible invoice.
options.reason: Saves roughly GBP 15-25/month of invoice but moves all state (database files and photos) onto a box the two developers must patch, back up, restore-test, and resize - about 2 extra complexity points, or ~GBP 480/month of engineering attention at the ~GBP 240/point model. It also exceeds the 4-point budget at 5. The answer changes if the invoice gap grows past the operational gap: managed pricing above ~GBP 500/month for this stack, or a dedicated ops hire raising the budget to 8.
trade_offs: Team owns backups, restore testing, disk-full, kernel patching, and TLS renewal
Single box is also the availability story: any incident is full downtime until a human intervenes

options.description: The conventional 'proper' stack: containers on an orchestration platform, load balancer, app replicas, managed Postgres, Redis cache, dedicated search engine, message broker for image jobs, CDN for photos.
options.reason: Every threshold that justifies these components is orders of magnitude away from the measured numbers: peak 0.28 RPS vs ~10+ single-instance comfort (replicas, balancer, orchestration); no key near 10 req/s and an idle origin (cache); ~1,000 recipes/year (search engine); ~6 jobs/day vs 500 jobs/s (broker); 11 GB/month egress vs a few hundred GB (CDN). It is 13 points against a budget of 4 and its high-end cost is 8x the stated GBP 50 budget. The measurements that would change the answer are exactly the revisit conditions on the rejected components.
trade_offs: Horizontal headroom and zero-downtime deploys nobody has asked for
3x the budget in complexity, 8x in money, carried continuously by 2 developers

availability.achievable: ~99.5% (single instance on a managed platform; minutes of downtime during deploys and platform incidents)
availability.explanation: No target was stated. A single managed instance with provider-managed database backups and PITR typically delivers around 99.5% observed. If a target of 99.9%+ is later stated, this design does not deliver it - see the load-balancer rejection trigger.

triggers.source: app admin dashboard, checked at the monthly product review
triggers.action: Re-run the capacity analysis end to end; at 50x current users, photo storage (~440 GB/year) and egress (~550 GB/month) become the material lines and the CDN and cost triggers below are likely to fire around the same time.
Profile the dominant queries and fix indexing first; re-evaluate a cache only with a measured statement of what load it would relieve.
Compute egress cost at the per-GB prices then in force and evaluate CDN/edge offload for photo delivery against it.
Review invoice line items against the GBP 50 budget before it breaches; identify which line is growing and re-run the relevant capacity calculation.

open_questions: Actual DAU share, session depth, and photo upload volume once launched - instrument basic analytics in week one so the assumed inputs become observed ones.
Typical uploaded photo size in practice (phone originals can be 5-12 MB); affects the storage line ~3x either way but no decision.
UK/EU users mean GDPR basics apply despite 'no compliance requirements': privacy policy, data deletion on request, hashed passwords. Not an architecture driver at this scale, but not optional either.
Are email notifications (e.g. on comments) expected? They fit the zero-cost database-backed jobs pattern; no component change either way.
